snip.t: The pain is pleuritic, worsens on deep inspiration, and is accompanied by mild dyspnoea.

| Heart failure (pulmonary oedema) | Orthopnoea, peripheral oedema, elevated JVP, bibasal crackles, rapid onset dyspnoea | BNP elevated, chest X‑ray shows Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly; cough is usually dry, not productive mucus‑laden |

Alveolar‑capillary membrane – thin type I pneumocytes for gas exchange, type II cells produce surfactant: Infection fills alveoli with exudate → loss of surfactant → atelectasis and impaired O₂ diffusion, producing hypoxaemia and dyspnoea.
HIV: Pneumococcus, TB, PCP (dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, very low saturation, bilateral "ground-glass" infiltrates)
Symptoms: progressive dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain (may disappear as fluid separates the pleura), dry cough; plus symptoms of the cause (fever, weight loss, orthopnoea).
A 68‑year‑old man with known ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF 30 %) presents with a 2‑week history of worsening dyspnoea on exertion and a dry, pleuritic left‑sided chest pain.
Air removal → sudden increase in pulmonary blood flow to previously collapsed alveoli → capillary leak → alveolar flooding → dyspnoea, pink frothy sputum.

| COPD | >40 y, long‑term smoking or biomass exposure; chronic productive cough, dyspnoea progressive, less diurnal variation | Fixed airflow obstruction (post‑bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC < 0.7) with < 12 % reversibility; emphysematous changes on CXR/CT |

qs.q: A 65-year-old heavy smoker presents with progressive dyspnoea, barrel chest, and minimal sputum production. His condition is primarily driven by an imbalance involving which protective substance?
qs.e: Emphysema is driven by a protease-antiprotease imbalance where a deficiency or inactivation of alpha-1 antitrypsin leads to unopposed elastase destruction of alveolar walls. Chronic bronchitis primarily involves mucous gland hyperplasia rather than primary antiprotease deficiency.

qs.q: A patient who underwent a lung transplant several months ago presents with progressive airflow obstruction and dyspnoea. Which form of chronic graft complication is the most likely cause?
qs.e: Bronchiolitis obliterans is the hallmark manifestation of chronic rejection in lung transplant recipients. The other options refer to adrenal pathologies rather than lung transplant complications.

qs.q: A 35-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with progressive dyspnoea, peripheral oedema, and cardiomegaly. Echocardiography demonstrates all four chambers dilated with predominant systolic contractile dysfunction and mural thrombi. What is the functional consequence of this condition?
o: Systolic dysfunction causing congestive heart failure
qs.e: Dilated cardiomyopathy causes systolic dysfunction and congestive heart failure where dilation predominates over hypertrophy. Diastolic dysfunction is characteristic of restrictive and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies.

qs.q: A young adult develops progressive dyspnoea and is found to have a genetic deficiency of alpha-1 antitrypsin. Which of the following morphological patterns of emphysema is most characteristically associated with this condition?
o: Centriacinar emphysema located in upper lobes
Paraseptal emphysema adjacent to the surface
qs.e: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes early-onset panacinar emphysema, which predominantly affects the lower lobes due to a protease-antiprotease imbalance. Centriacinar emphysema is typically smoking-related and affects the upper lobes.

qs.q: An industrial worker with a history of heavy exposure to silica dust presents with progressive dyspnoea. Chest radiography reveals upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis and egg-shell calcification of the hilar lymph nodes. This patient is at a significantly increased risk for developing which of the following secondary infections?
qs.e: Silicosis is specifically associated with an increased risk of developing tuberculosis due to impaired macrophage function. The other listed pathogens are not the primary specific risk associated with silica exposure.

qs.q: A 60-year-old patient presents with the classical symptomatic triad of exertional dyspnoea, angina, and syncope. Which valvular lesion is most consistent with this presentation?
qs.e: The classical triad of exertional dyspnoea, angina, and syncope is characteristic of aortic stenosis once symptoms supervene. Mitral regurgitation symptoms are typically dominated by features of congestive cardiac failure.

qs.q: A young male develops sudden dyspnoea, absent right breath sounds, tracheal deviation to the left, and rapidly falling blood pressure. The immediately life-threatening mechanism is
o: Tension pneumothorax — ball-valve air leak causing mediastinal shift and circulatory collapse
Spontaneous oesophageal rupture with mediastinal emphysema and pleural contamination
Massive haemothorax from intercostal vessel laceration compressing the lung
Massive pulmonary embolism causing acute right-sided heart failure
qs.e: Tension pneumothorax occurs when a ball-valve leak allows air into but not out of the pleural space — the resulting mediastinal shift compresses the pulmonary circulation and can cause rapid death.
